overview.title: 📖 Overview: Anatomy, Symbolism, and Sunlight
overview.subtitle: Tamid 31a–31b
overview.hebrewSource: יָד וָרֶגֶל, כַּעֲקֵידַת יִצְחָק בֶּן אַבְרָהָם
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The mishna walks through the daily lamb's flaying and dismemberment in exacting anatomical detail — which limb comes off in which order, which priest carries which piece, and even how each priest holds his portion as the line of nine forms. The Gemara then explains why the lamb's legs were bound only in pairs (foreleg to hind leg) rather than all four together, comparing it to the binding of Isaac, and debates whether the reason is dignity or avoiding pagan custom. A description of the Temple's thirteen specialized tables follows, along with the practical reason marble was preferred over precious metal for handling meat. The daf closes by explaining why the morning and afternoon daily offerings were slaughtered at different corners of the altar — always 'opposite the sun.'

slides.title: 🔪 Flaying and Dismembering the Lamb
slides.subtitle: A precise sequence, hook by hook, cut by cut

steps.content: 1️⃣ The priest punctures the hind legs at the knee joints (never breaking a bone) and hangs the animal from two hooks to begin flaying
2️⃣ He flays downward to the breast, then severs the head and the lower legs, handing each to its designated carrier
3️⃣ He completes the flaying, cuts open the heart to drain its blood, then removes the forelegs and the right hind leg (with both testicles)
4️⃣ With the animal now hanging only from its left hind leg, he tears open the midsection, exposing all the innards

5️⃣ He carefully separates the lung from the liver and the liver's lobe — WITHOUT moving any organ from its natural position — then removes breast, flanks (leaving the spine untouched), the cud (with windpipe/heart/lung attached), and finally the haunch and remaining leg

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: All nine priests assigned to carry limbs now stand in a line, each holding his designated piece, ready to ascend to the altar.

slides.title: 🙌 Nine Priests, Nine Precise Positions
slides.subtitle: Exactly how each carrier held his portion
rows: Head (right hand) + right hind leg (left hand)
Horns between fingers, fats placed over the slaughter site to conceal it
Haunch (right hand, tail dangling with liver-lobe and kidneys) + left hind leg (left hand)
Innards (in a vessel), fine flour, griddle-cakes, wine
Carried separately to the western side of the ramp, then salted

slides.title: 🐏 Why Not Tie All Four Legs Together?
slides.subtitle: A dispute over dignity vs. avoiding pagan custom

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: The foreleg and hind leg are bound together — 'like the binding of Isaac, son of Abraham' — evoking that foundational moment of sacrifice.

lines.speaker: Rav Huna
lines.text: Tying all four legs together is avoided because it would constitute a DEGRADATION of consecrated items — an undignified way to handle a sacred offering.

lines.speaker: Rav Ḥisda
lines.text: Rather, it's avoided because that specific method of binding was associated with pagan ritual practice — following it would violate 'you shall not walk in their statutes' (Leviticus 18:3).

lines.speaker: Practical difference
lines.text: If one tied the animal with SILK or a thread of GOLD — not degrading, but still resembling pagan custom — the two opinions would disagree on whether it's permitted.

slides.title: 🍽️ Thirteen Tables, Each With Its Purpose
slides.subtitle: Marble, silver, and gold — chosen deliberately, not by default
rows: In the slaughterhouse, north of the altar — for rinsing the innards
West of the ramp — marble held the limbs before ascent; silver held the 93 daily service vessels
Inside the Entrance Hall — silver received the incoming shewbread, gold received it on its way OUT (since sanctity only rises, never descends)
Inside the Sanctuary itself — the permanent Table for the shewbread

callout.label: Why marble at all, given Temple wealth?
callout.text: Rav Ḥinnana (citing Rabbi Asi, citing Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzḥak): metal tables would get scalding hot in the sun and could damage the sacrificial limbs — marble stays cool, protecting the meat.

slides.title: ☀️ 'Two by Day' — Slaughtered Opposite the Sun
slides.subtitle: Deriving why morning and afternoon offerings use different altar corners
slides.label: The derivation:
slides.text: Numbers 28:3 says the daily offerings are 'two by day' — since the daily-obligation aspect is already covered by the next verse ('one lamb in the morning, the other in the afternoon'), this extra phrase must teach something more: that each lamb is slaughtered directly opposite the sunlight. Since the sun tracks from east to west across the southern sky (Israel's latitude), the MORNING offering is slaughtered at the altar's NORTHWEST corner (facing the rising eastern sun), and the AFTERNOON offering at the NORTHEAST corner (facing the setting western sun) — always positioned in full daylight, never in the altar's shadow.

summary.principle: Every stage of the daily offering — the flaying sequence, each priest's exact grip on his limb, the choice of binding method, the specific materials of thirteen distinct tables, and even which corner of the altar caught the sunlight — reflects a service where practical wisdom, textual derivation, and symbolic meaning were woven together into a single, precise choreography.

flowSteps.content: 🔪 Flaying and dismemberment proceed in strict order, organs left undisturbed in their natural positions
🙌 Nine priests line up, each holding his designated limb in a precisely specified grip
🐏 Legs bound only in pairs — dignity or avoiding pagan custom, per Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda

columns.content: 🍽️ Thirteen tables, each material chosen for practical and halakhic reasons

quiz.q: How did the priest suspend the daily lamb in order to flay it, according to the mishna?
o: By tying a rope around its neck
By puncturing the hind legs at the knee and hanging the animal from two hooks
By breaking its leg and hanging it by the bone
By using a special sling
quiz.e: The mishna specifies that the priest would not break the leg in the ordinary manner but would puncture it at the knee joint and suspend the animal from hooks placed through those holes.

quiz.q: According to the baraita, what does the binding of the lamb's foreleg to its hind leg evoke?
o: The Exodus from Egypt
The binding of Isaac, son of Abraham (Akeidat Yitzchak)
The revelation at Mount Sinai
The dedication of the Tabernacle
quiz.e: The baraita explicitly describes this binding method as being 'like the binding of Isaac, son of Abraham,' invoking that foundational moment of sacrifice.

quiz.q: What are the two explanations offered by Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda for why the lamb's legs were not all tied together?
o: Cost and practicality
One says it would be a degradation of consecrated items; the other says it would resemble a pagan ritual practice, violating 'you shall not walk in their statutes'
Both agree it was simply for convenience
Neither offers any halakhic reason
quiz.e: Rav Huna attributes the practice to avoiding degradation of sacred items, while Rav Ḥisda attributes it to avoiding imitation of gentile ritual customs.

quiz.q: Why were eight of the Temple's thirteen tables made of marble rather than gold or silver, despite the principle that 'there is no poverty in a place of wealth'?
o: Marble was simply cheaper
Metal tables would become scalding hot in the sun and could damage the sacrificial limbs, while marble stayed cool
Gold and silver were reserved only for the Holy of Holies
There is no explanation given in the text
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that metal heats up excessively in the sun, which could harm the meat, whereas marble remains cool — a practical reason overriding the general preference for lavish materials.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's derivation from 'two by day' (Numbers 28:3), why were the morning and afternoon daily offerings slaughtered at different corners of the altar?
o: To commemorate the two tablets of the Ten Commandments
Each was slaughtered directly opposite the sunlight — the morning offering at the northwest corner facing the rising sun, the afternoon offering at the northeast corner facing the setting sun
It was purely a matter of convenience for the priests
There is no halakhic reason; it was random
quiz.e: The Gemara derives from the extra phrase 'two by day' that each offering must be slaughtered in direct sunlight, which — given the sun's path — requires different altar corners for morning versus afternoon.
